title: Startup variance and KV-cache repopulation across SKUs
body:
Summary:
This note documents an experimental sweep focused on the cost and latency impact of KV-cache repopulation during service startup and after cache invalidation across a sample set of cloud GPU SKUs (A100, H100, L40S) and driver/CUDA combinations. The goal: quantify how much extra latency and token-cost is incurred when a serving process receives requests with cold KV caches, and to determine SKU-specific mitigation strategies (warmup prefill, background prefetch, pre-warming instances).

Motivation / Problem statement:
We observe non-trivial p99 latency spikes and higher per-token cost for sessions that hit the service after long idle periods or after model reloads. Root cause hypothesis: when the KV cache is cold, prefill requests (the prefix) must be decoded and populated into KV memory; this can induce extra kernel launches, memory copies, and reduced parallelism for the first few decode steps. Different GPUs and interconnects (NVLink vs PCIe) show different amortization curves. Driver/CUDA versions appear to change kernel launch latency and warmup jitter.

Experiment plan (high-level):
- SKUs tested: g4A (A100 40GB), g5H (H100 80GB), g6L (L40S 48GB) — anonymized cloud labels to match our fleet naming.
- CUDA / driver combos: CUDA 11.8 + driver 535, CUDA 12.1 + driver 545, CUDA 12.2 + driver 550 (selected because customer fleets span these).
- Models: medium-sized LLaMA derivative (7B-ish prefilled length 256), and a 13B config (prefill 512). Both use kv-cache enabled decoding path and fp16 execution.
- Workload: synthetic real-user trace replay with realistic prefix distribution (mix of short 40–80 token prompts and long 400+ token prompts). For cold cache experiments we explicitly invalidate KV state between sessions and issue a warmup-prefill variant.
- Metrics: first-request tail latencies (p50/p95/p99), per-token CPU/GPU kernel count for first 64 decode steps, tokens/sec after steady-state, cumulative extra tokens decoded (wasted) during repopulation, memory copies (GB), and energy proxy (W*s via telemetry).

Test harness and instrumentation:
- Built a harness that collects per-kernel timestamps via CUPTI and our eBPF-based tracing to attribute stalls to memcpy vs kernel launch vs kernel runtime.
- We added a small shim to the runtime that logs: session_id, warmup_phase (cold|warm), step_index, kernel_name, start_ns, end_ns, memcpy_bytes, cpu_thread. Outputs were aggregated into CSVs for analysis.
- Each SKU/CUDA pair run for 8 hours to capture diurnal noise; we repeated experiments 3x per condition and trimmed outliers.

Key findings (numbers averaged across runs, 7B model unless noted):
1) First-decode p99 penalty: A100: +120ms, H100: +75ms, L40S: +200ms (relative to warm steady-state per-token decode).
2) Kernel-launch dominated on PCIe-path SKUs (A100/L40S) when CUDA 11.8 drivers used; upgraded CUDA 12.2 reduced per-kernel launch latencies by ~18% on all SKUs.
3) KV repopulation step-count overhead: first 32 decoding steps saw 1.7x more kernel calls on cold sessions vs warm (due to prefill replays and smaller, fragmented launches). This effect softened after ~48 steps for H100 but persisted to ~80 steps on L40S.
4) NVLink advantage: H100 instances with NVLink showed ~2x fewer host-device memcpy stalls during repopulation due to larger peer-to-peer bandwidth used for cross-GPU KV rebuilds, reducing wallclock repopulation time.
5) Memory-bound stalls: L40S showed repeated GDDR refresh/clock-throttle events under sustained repopulation bursts (linked to SKU clock governors). Those drives produced occasional 30–50ms micro-pauses that inflated p99.
6) Driver sensitivity: driver 535 + CUDA 11.8 had more frequent small (~2–8ms) jitter spikes attributed to context-switch/relaunch overhead; driver 550 reduced these but introduced a rare (~200ms) single-step stall in one run (need to profile further).
7) Small prefix amplification: sessions that had long prefill (400 tokens) followed by short decode (10 tokens) were disproportionately affected because repopulation work did not amortize. End-to-end latency for such sessions on L40S was up to 3x baseline.

Representative data table (median across runs) — textual form:
- A100 (CUDA11.8/driver535): p50 extra 48ms, p95 extra 90ms, p99 extra 120ms, steady tokens/sec 620, first-64-kernel-count +70%
- H100 (CUDA12.2/driver550): p50 extra 30ms, p95 extra 55ms, p99 extra 75ms, steady tokens/sec 830, first-64-kernel-count +35%
- L40S (CUDA11.8/driver535): p50 extra 65ms, p95 extra 140ms, p99 extra 200ms, steady tokens/sec 540, first-64-kernel-count +95%

Qualitative observations / traces:
- On A100 under older drivers the GPU would frequently execute many tiny kernels during repopulation (launch-time dominated). Flame graphs showed long stacks of kernel-launchs with <50us runtime each but ~100us launch overhead.
- H100 NVLink runs often overlapped KV copy + compute, thanks to our runtime using peer-access to build distributed caches; this overlap greatly reduces visible latency spikes.
- L40S runs exposed a sensitivity to PCIe root-complex placement; instances with non-local NVMe/NUMA placements had higher host->device scatter and more memcpy stalls.

Interventions tested and impact:
- Background prefetch: spawn a low-priority background task that pre-decodes common prefix tokens for hot models. Reduced p99 penalty by ~40% on A100 and ~55% on L40S, negligible change on H100 (already low).
- Aggressive kernel fusion (runtime change): fusing the small kernels that handle attention score compute for the first N steps reduced kernel-count overhead ~60% and p99 by ~20% across all SKUs (complexity cost in codegen).
- Pre-warmed pool (instance-level): keeping a small number of instances warm with KV populated eliminated the cold penalty entirely for those sessions, but increases idle cost — economical only for high-SLA customers.
- Driver upgrade to CUDA12.2: universally improved kernel-launchs and reduced jitter; single rare stall observed on H100 needs follow-up with vendor.

Cost-amortization model (rough):
- For a long-prefill session (400 tokens), the extra wallclock to repopulate KV is ~350–900ms depending on SKU. If the application issues >=20 decode tokens after that prefill, amortized cost per token becomes <5% extra. For chat-ish flows with frequent short replies (<10 tokens), the amortization is poor and cold sessions are expensive.

Recommendations (short-term):
1) Upgrade fleet drivers to CUDA12.2 where possible but pilot H100s for the rare driver stall. File vendor ticket with trace + CUPTI logs. (Owner: Ravi)
2) Implement background prefetch for customer models with known hot prefixes. Start as an opt-in toggle in Dedicated and Private. (Owner: Harper)
3) Add instance-level placement check to ensure PCIe locality for L40S (avoid bad root complexes). Expand node tagging in infra. (Owner: Platform Eng)
4) Add telemetry metric: "kv_repop_steps" and tag by sku/driver so we can alert on sudden increases. (Owner: SRE)
5) Build a quick cost model into Console: show estimated cold-session penalty for a given prompt length and expected reply length to help customers decide pre-warm vs pay-as-you-go. (Owner: Product-hosted-api)

Longer-term suggestions:
- Kernel fusion and codegen optimizations targeted at first-N-steps for common model architectures. This is moderately invasive but yields good cross-sku wins.
- Explore persistently cached prefix shards (on-device) that survive short-lived model reloads to avoid full repopulation for common prefixes.
- Work with cloud vendors on root-complex placement and NVLink topologies for L40S variants; document SKU-specific best practices in our support docs.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Why did driver 550 produce the single-step 200ms stall on H100? Need vendor-assisted trace analysis.
- Can we instrument runtime to opportunistically fuse kernels at JIT time only for first-N steps? Proof-of-concept ticket exists GH:repo/runtime-warmup#158.
- For multi-tenant Dedicated nodes, does background prefetch risk noisy neighbor amplification? Need isolation study.

Experiment artifacts and how to reproduce (short):
1) Checkout GH:repo/runtime-warmup branch warmup-sweep.
2) Start harness: ./scripts/run_kv_repop_sweep.sh --model llama-7b --sku g5h --cuda 12.2 --duration 8h --invalidate-every 300s
3) Aggregation: python tools/aggregate_warmup.py --input out/*.csv --output analysis/g5h-12.2.csv
4) Postprocess: notebooks/warmup-amortization.ipynb (contains plotting cells used to compute the tables above).

Notes to reviewers:
- I intentionally focused on observable runtime-level signals (kernel counts, memcpy size, per-step timing) rather than higher-level RPC metrics to isolate hardware/driver effects. We should follow up with a production sampling that correlates these signals with actual customer traces (privacy-safe sampling).
- The results are noisy; I've attached raw CSVs to GH artifacts and JIRA ticket SRV-987 for further triage.
